sentences.text: Megalolamna could reach a maximum length of 5.1 meters, a size similar to the modern great white shark, though a more conservative estimate places the largest known specimen at an average of 5.1 meters.

The teeth featured a pointed main cusp, upward-pointing lateral cusplets of similar size, and a strongly bilobed root, with the largest known tooth measuring 4.5 cm in height while the smallest measured 8.2 mm.
The species name paradoxodon means 'paradoxical tooth' and refers to the unusual appearance of the shark's teeth.
The genus name Megalolamna combines the Greek word for 'big' with the name of the genus Lamna.

The genus Megalolamna was formally described in 2016 by Kensu Shimada and colleagues based on five fossil teeth found in the US, Japan, and Peru, and the only known species in the genus is Megalolamna paradoxodon.
The holotype for Megalolamna is a complete tooth cataloged as UCMP 112146, discovered in Kern County, California.
A 2024 study extended the known time range of Megalolamna to the Late Oligocene (23.5 million years ago) based on a tooth from South Carolina.
Teeth found in Maryland represent the northernmost known occurrences of Megalolamna.
The first tooth of this species was described in 1879 by Josef Probst as Otodus serotinus from a fossil found in Baltringen, Germany.

Despite its size, Megalolamna fed only on medium-sized prey, using its front teeth to seize prey and lateral corner teeth to cut it, suggesting researchers believe it seized prey with front teeth and then cut it with lateral teeth at the mouth corners to fit it for swallowing.

Fossil evidence indicates that Megalolamna had a cosmopolitan distribution, and the geographical distribution of Megalolamna is similar to that of modern lamniform sharks like the goblin shark, megamouth shark, and Bigeye sand tiger.
Most Megalolamna fossils come from shallow marine environments, though some suggest it also lived in cold, subtropical waters.
Megalolamna belongs to the family Otodontidae, which includes the megalodon, and is considered the sister genus to Otodus.

Megalolamna lived from the Late Oligocene to the Middle Miocene, approximately 23.5 to 15 million years ago, dating to the Miocene epoch, and specifically from the Rupelian to the Messinian stages, between 33.9 and 5.333 million years ago.

Fossils of Megalolamna have been found in the Americas, Europe, and Japan, and the species had a cosmopolitan distribution and primarily inhabited shallow waters from tropical to mid-latitude regions, with fossils found in early Miocene strata in Peru, Japan, California, and North Carolina.
It remains uninvestigated whether the specific names Otodus serotinus and Lamna bassanii are synonyms.
It is debated whether Megalolamna had one or multiple rows of teeth, as its dentition shows a continuous series without clear differences between upper and lower jaws.
Researchers note that the relationship between Megalolamna and Otodus is problematic due to a 43-million-year gap in their appearance.
